records.sourceFile: Effects of rehabilitation interventions on time to return to play and reinjury rate in athletes with acute hamstring strain injuries.pdf

paper.citation: Zhu J, Huang S, Luo S, Huo X, Zheng L, Grecic D, et al. Effects of rehabilitation interventions on time to return to play and reinjury rate in athletes with acute hamstring strain injuries. Scientific Reports. 2026;16:30859.
paper.abstract: Fourteen randomized controlled trials (693 athletes) were pooled to compare rehabilitation approaches for acute hamstring strain, with time to return to play (TTRTP) as the primary outcome and re-injury as the secondary outcome. A lengthening-focused protocol may shorten TTRTP with moderate certainty, while progressive agility and trunk stabilization, PRP, rESWT and LLLT remain uncertain for re-injury, and pain-threshold rehabilitation enhanced strength without delaying TTRTP.
paper.tldr: A lengthening-focused eccentric protocol may shorten return to play after acute hamstring strain, supported by two trials with moderate certainty. Re-injury benefits from add-on approaches such as PATS, PRP and shockwave therapy are inconclusive or low certainty.
paper.methods: Six databases (PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase and Google Scholar) were searched from inception to January 2026 for English-language RCTs of rehabilitation in athletes with acute hamstring strain. Risk of bias was rated with RoB 2 and certainty with GRADE, with random-effects models where clinical transitivity was judged adequate and trial sequential analysis as a robustness check.
paper.findings: L-protocol (two trials, 131 athletes): TTRTP WMD -28.29 days (95% CI -41.60 to -14.99); re-injury RD -0.05 (95% CI -0.11 to 0.02), not significant. PATS (two trials): TTRTP WMD -6.72 days (95% CI -16.81 to 3.36), not significant; re-injury RD -0.35 (95% CI -0.74 to 0.03), inconclusive, with Peto OR 0.08 in sensitivity analysis. PRP with rehabilitation (three trials): TTRTP WMD -6.77 days (95% CI -10.79 to -2.75; I2 = 70%); re-injury RD -0.08 (95% CI -0.19 to 0.02), not significant. Single trials: rESWT shortened TTRTP by 2.90 days versus sham (95% CI -5.63 to -0.17); LLLT did not differ from placebo; pain-threshold rehabilitation did not change TTRTP versus pain-free rehabilitation (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.40 to 1.40) and gave greater knee flexor strength recovery at 90 degrees hip and knee flexion (mean difference 15%, 95% CI 1 to 28%).
paper.limitations: Heterogeneity reached 72% for re-injury, blinding was not possible in exercise trials, and re-injury events were sparse, so TSA did not reach the required information size for PATS or PRP re-injury. Return-to-play definitions and re-injury follow-up (2 to 24 months) varied, and most trials used elite or professional male samples, with female and recreational athletes underrepresented. One included master's thesis (Dhlamini et al., PEDro 4) was used only in narrative synthesis. The Discussion calls the PATS RD of 35% clinically meaningful but also says it should not be read as evidence of efficacy; this summary follows the Results and GRADE conclusions. The protocol was registered after the search was completed, and the authors' post-hoc split of physical modalities is noted. The text reports PRP TTRTP heterogeneity as I2 = 70% in the Results but 62% in the GRADE text. The stated range of mean ages (20.3 to 46.6 years) does not match Table 2, where the highest group mean is about 30 years.
paper.practicalImplications: When getting an athlete back quickly is the priority after an acute hamstring strain, a lengthening-focused eccentric protocol is the best-supported option in this review, based on two mostly elite male trials. Do not rely on PATS, PRP or shockwave therapy to reduce re-injury: those results are inconclusive or rest on one or two small trials.
paper.athleteDev: The one trial with a strength outcome for pain-threshold rehabilitation found a 15% greater knee flexor strength gain at 90 degrees hip and knee flexion, with no slowing of return, under the authors' rule of pain 4/10 or less that settles within 24 hours. The PATS trial found no between-group difference in hop tests or 40-yard sprint times, so the review does not show a sprint or performance benefit from these programs.
paper.rtp: The review informs timing only in part: the L-protocol was associated with earlier return to play, but the trials used varied return criteria and the authors warn that TTRTP is not a marker of full recovery. Clearance in the PATS trial still left residual symptoms in many athletes and no MRI-complete healing, so the review cannot set return-to-sport criteria; strength, neuromuscular control and sport-specific function should be checked as well.
